intro: Grow a population and watch its curve. Start with unlimited resources (the J-curve), add a carrying capacity (the S-curve), then let the herd overshoot it and crash. Survivorship curves and r- and K-selection each have their own view, because they answer different questions: when individuals die, and how they reproduce.
howItWorks:
The model steps one year at a time. Exponential: N grows by r × N each year. Logistic: by r × N × (1 − N/K), so growth slows as N nears K. Overshoot: the herd responds to its numbers two years earlier (crowding takes time to bite), so it passes K; once above K it overgrazes, and the range then supports fewer (K drops to about 55% of its first value).

Doubling time uses the rule of 70 (70 ÷ the growth rate in percent), the same recipe as the course questions (ApEnvCalc). Survivorship curves are the idealized Type I, II and III shapes on a log scale. Numbers in the drills are invented for practice and recomputed by a checker on 300 problems per scenario.

contexts.lead: A herd of {n0} deer is brought to an island with no predators in {y0}. With plenty of food it grows {rate}% a year.
Zebra mussels reach a lake in {y0}. Divers estimate {n0} mussels per square meter, growing {rate}% a year.
A city of {n0} people in {y0} grows {rate}% a year.
Yeast cells grow in a flask of sugar water that is never refilled.
Bluegill are stocked in a new farm pond.
Reindeer are brought to an island with rich lichen and no predators.
Hunters remove the wolves and mountain lions from a plateau, and the deer herd grows.
In a wealthy country, nearly every baby survives childhood, and most people die after age 70.
contexts.why: Few offspring, a lot of care, and good health care: most live a long life and deaths come late.

contexts.lead: An elephant calf is protected by its whole herd for years, and most elephants live past 50.
contexts.why: One calf at a time with years of care: most survive to old age, then deaths rise.

contexts.lead: Banding studies show that a songbird population loses about the same share of its members each year, young or old, mostly to predators.
contexts.why: About the same share dies each year at every age, so the curve on a log scale is a straight line.

contexts.lead: An oyster releases millions of eggs into the water. Almost all of the larvae are eaten or swept away, but an oyster that settles on a reef can live 20 years.
contexts.why: Huge numbers of young and no care: almost all die young; the few survivors live long.

contexts.lead: A sea turtle lays about 100 eggs per nest and leaves. Hatchlings are eaten on the beach and in the sea, but an adult may live 50 years or more.
contexts.why: Many eggs and no care: deaths are heaviest in the first weeks; adults survive well.

contexts.name: Field mouse
contexts.lead: A small rodent of farm fields:
traits: 4 to 6 litters a year of about 6 young each
young are on their own at 3 weeks
contexts.why: early breeding, many litters and little care.

contexts.name: Dandelion
traits: one plant makes thousands of wind-blown seeds
contexts.why: many small seeds, early reproduction and fast spread.

contexts.name: Albatross
traits: first breeds at 5 to 10 years old
lays one egg every one or two years
both parents feed the chick for months
contexts.why: late breeding, one egg at a time and a lot of care.

contexts.name: Humpback whale
traits: the mother nurses the calf for about a year
first breeds at about 5 to 10 years
contexts.why: few, large young with long care and late breeding.
